long term priming in the posture decision task is (i) independent of the identity of human figures (Experiment 1), (ii) independent of the depth orientation of body postures (Experiments 1 and 2), but (iii) dependent on the variability of the body postures in the priming and the test phase (Experiment 3).

long term priming in the posture decision task is invariant to the exact appearance of the human figure (Experiment 1), is independent of depth orientation (Experiment 2), and depends on the variability of the posture representations in the priming and the test phase (Experiment 3).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how human observers can identify body postures.
the nature of the representations that support human posture recognition.
the question how the human visual system represents body postures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
priming of body posture representations depends on the spatial relations between body parts and not on the identity of the body.
the long term priming in the posture recognition task is based on the activation of high level posture representation that are abstracted from the identity of the actor.

the long term priming effect is not based on the activation of a specific posture representation but on the reactivation (or retrieval) of a general posture representation that is flexible with regard to identity and depth orientation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

human posture representations are highly abstract in the sense that they are invariant to the exact visual appearance or identity of the actor and the orientation of the body parts in the depth direction.
the visual system is able to flexibly tune its representations of the human body in order to optimize performance in the task at hand (e.g. posture identification).

the long term priming effect in our posture recognition task reflects an abstract representation of body postures that is independent of the identity of a person and that is based on a flexible set of posture representations that are sensitive to depth orientation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
human posture representations are highly flexible in terms of the identity of actors involved and the depth orientation of postures.
the human brain is very good in representing the spatial relations between body parts in the absence of any information regarding the person in the posture.

human body posture representations can be flexibly tuned to a large range of visual appearances of human figures and are therefore well suited for the representation and recognition of human postures.
